title: Who to call and what to say
disclaimer: DRAFT, not reviewed, not medical or legal advice. Needs review by a qualified paediatric reviewer before any use in an app. Scope: children from about 1 year to puberty; infant (under 1) steps differ and are not covered here.

items.text: Breathing has stopped or is laboured, or the child has trouble speaking.
Lips or skin turn blue, purple or grey, or look pale or blotchy.
The child cannot be roused, is limp and floppy, or seems unaware of what is going on; or alertness is dropping, or behaviour is strange or withdrawn.
Any seizure (rhythmic jerking with loss of responsiveness).
Bleeding you cannot control, or a deep or gaping wound or burn.
Choking on something you cannot dislodge.
A serious allergic reaction.
A head injury followed by lower alertness, confusion, headache, vomiting, irritability or trouble walking.
Suspected neck, back or pelvis injury: call and keep the child still.
A child pulled out of water who does not respond.
Fever together with abnormal appearance, breathing or circulation; or a stiff neck with headache and fever; or a purple or red rash that is spreading fast.
Vomiting blood, significant blood in stool, or signs of significant dehydration (sunken eyes, no tears or urine, lethargy).
Severe or increasing pain anywhere, or a heat or cold injury such as heat exhaustion or frostbite.
A child who has swallowed poison or too much medicine and has collapsed, is seizing, is struggling to breathe or cannot be woken. UK: 999 for any swallowed poison or overdose.

Burn emergencies: a burn that is large (about the size of the child's palm or bigger) or deep; a burn on the face, hands, genitals or bottom; an electrical or chemical burn; skin that looks charred, leathery, white, brown or black, or has no feeling; breathing trouble, smoke or fume exposure, confusion or difficulty waking; or you are not sure how serious it is.
More than one child hurt or seriously ill at the same time.
You are not sure what is wrong but believe the child is in danger. The operator will guide you.
Go to the emergency room, or call 911 for an ambulance, for severe injury or life-threatening illness. An ambulance is safer than driving a seriously ill or injured child yourself.

Emergency room list: wounds that keep bleeding, a seizure lasting more than 2 minutes in a child who has never had one (call emergency services for any seizure), head injury with changed behaviour, loss of consciousness, severe belly pain, severe burns, swallowed object with trouble breathing or swallowing, severe fractures, trouble breathing, vomiting or coughing blood, severe neck stiffness or rash with fever, poisoning, worsening asthma or diabetes.
A baby under 60 days (about 2 months) with a fever above 100.4 F needs emergency care now. (Infants are outside this guide's scope.)

Burns: call emergency services for a burn that is large (about the size of the child's palm or bigger) or deep; a burn on the face, hands, genitals or bottom; an electrical or chemical burn; skin that looks charred, leathery, white, brown or black, or has no feeling; breathing trouble, smoke or fume exposure, confusion or difficulty waking; or you are not sure how serious it is. A blistering or swollen burn bigger than the child's hand, or any burn on a foot or over a joint, should be seen immediately by a paediatrician or in an emergency room.

UK: go to A&E for a cut where bleeding will not stop with pressure, spurting blood, an embedded object, or a very large or deep wound; do not drive yourself if you are the injured person (ask someone else or call 999).
UK: a suspected broken arm or leg, if the child cannot use the limb, goes to A&E. If you cannot move the child without pain, call 999.

Child may have swallowed, breathed in, or got on skin or in eyes a medicine, chemical or other possible poison, even if the child looks fine. US: call Poison Help, 1-800-222-1222. It is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, and it connects to your regional poison centre.
If the child is unwell, or you believe the child is in danger, call 911 rather than waiting for the poison line.
poison.org offers a free online tool, but call the phone line for pregnancy, babies under 6 months, adults over 79, several substances at once, or self-harm.

Do not wait for symptoms before getting poison advice. Australia: call the Poisons Information Line; call 000 if someone has stopped breathing, collapsed, had a seizure, had a severe allergic reaction or has been exposed to a harmful substance. Canada: get advice from a poison information centre or call 911 right away; if the child shows any signs of illness, altered awareness or anything else that makes you immediately concerned, call 911 or your local ambulance service.
If the child has collapsed, is having a seizure, has trouble breathing or cannot be woken, call 911 (or the local emergency number) instead of the poison line.
Have the product, container or medicine package in hand when you call.
Do not try to make the child vomit.
UK: if you think a child has swallowed, touched or breathed in something harmful, call 999 or go to A&E (do not drive yourself). If you are not sure whether it is harmful, call NHS 111.
UK: a swallowed button battery or magnet means 999 or A&E straight away.
Not an emergency and you are unsure where to go: call the child's own paediatrician or doctor, including after hours (many offices give advice by phone).

Problems suitable for a call to the paediatrician first: minor burns, ear pain, pink eye, possible urinary infection, sore throat, rashes, vomiting or diarrhoea with mild dehydration, simple wounds, objects stuck in ear or nose, colds, coughs and allergies. Minor means minor: a serious burn or severe allergic reaction is an emergency.
A rough test: if the child can walk, talk, interact and play, it is probably not an emergency (still ask if unsure).

Needs prompt same-day medical advice but not an ambulance: fever in a child who looks more than mildly ill, severe vomiting or diarrhoea, a cut that may need stitches, animal bites that break the skin.
UK: NHS 111 is for urgent problems that are not emergencies; for a child under 5 use the phone, not the online service.
Australia: healthdirect nurse line 1800 022 222 (registered nurse, 24 hours).
Where you are: the exact address, nearest cross street or landmark. Mobile calls may not be located automatically, so be ready to say it.
What happened and the main problem (for example: not breathing, seizure, bleeding).
The child's age, whether the child is awake and whether the child is breathing; the operator may also ask about medical history.
A phone number they can call you back on (and if a mobile call drops, give your number).
Stay on the line until the rescue crew arrives, unless the operator tells you that you can hang up. They may coach you through first aid or CPR or tell you to move somewhere safer.
Make a voice call rather than texting if you can safely do so (in Australia you cannot text 000 at all). Put the phone on speaker so your hands are free.
Be patient and answer the questions calmly, slowly and clearly; the questions let responders send the right kind of help.
Do not hang up, even if you think the call was a mistake.

While waiting: stay with the child, turn on lights (inside and outside) and unlock the front door so responders can get in, open curtains, lock pets away (hazard lights if in a car), and call again if the child's condition or your location changes.
For the crew: tell them about known allergies, and if it was given, the time any emergency medicine such as epinephrine was given.
Your street address, posted by the home phone.
The child's paediatrician or GP name and contact details.
A list of the child's regular medicines (and bring the medicines with the child to hospital).
Known allergies (to tell the paramedics).
For a suspected poisoning: the product, medicine bottle or packet, what it was, how much, when and how it happened (swallowed, breathed in, skin or eye), and what symptoms there are.
Any care plan the child has (some conditions in a care plan require the parent to be told).
Check it is safe for you to approach before you go to the child. Do not move an injured child unless staying put is dangerous (for example fire).
Check if the child responds: call out their name and tap the shoulder. Do not shake. Shout for help.
If there is no response or it is a serious emergency, have someone call the emergency number straight away, or call yourself with the phone on speaker.

Open the airway and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than about 10 seconds; gasping is not normal breathing. Airway: lift the chin and tilt the head back, UNLESS a neck or back injury is possible; then lift the jaw forward without tilting the head (see step 9).

Child not responding but breathing normally, and no neck or back injury is suspected: place them in the recovery position (on their side, head tilted back), call emergency services, stay with them and keep checking breathing. If a neck or back injury is suspected, do not roll them: see step 9.

Child not responding and not breathing normally: start CPR and send someone for a defibrillator (AED) if there is one. Cycle of 30 chest compressions then 2 breaths; push on the centre of the chest about 5 cm (2 inches) deep, 100 to 120 per minute, let the chest rise fully. In the US start with the 30 compressions; in the UK start with 5 rescue breaths first. Do not check for a pulse. Continue until help takes over or the child breathes normally.
If you cannot or will not give breaths, keep giving chest compressions.

If you are alone with a child who is not responding and not breathing normally: if you have a phone, put it on speaker and call emergency services NOW, then start CPR and follow the operator. If you have NO phone, do about 1 minute of CPR and then go to call. Take a small child with you if you can (unless a neck or back injury is suspected). If anyone else is there, they call straight away while you start CPR.

Suspected neck, back or pelvis injury: call emergency services. Do not move the child and do not tell them to move unless they are in immediate danger. Kneel at their head and hold it with both hands so head, neck and back stay in line. If they are not responding, open the airway by lifting the jaw forward without tilting the head. If they are not breathing, start CPR at once. If they are not responding but are breathing, keep holding the head steady, keep checking their breathing and wait for help; only if you cannot keep the airway open, use the spinal recovery position. If you must move them, two people should move the child so the head and neck do not twist.

Severe bleeding: press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing; shout for someone to call emergency services, or if you are alone put the phone on speaker and call while you keep pressing. If blood soaks through, put more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is stuck in the wound, leave it and press firmly on either side of it.
Stay with the child, stay as calm as you can (children copy you), and keep the phone line open until told otherwise.

signs: Trouble breathing or swallowing, wheezing, chest or throat tightness, hoarse voice
Swelling of lips, tongue or face
Hives or rash together with any breathing, dizziness or stomach symptoms
Pale, blue or grey skin or lips, weak pulse, dizziness, fainting
Vomiting or diarrhoea, confusion or unusual drowsiness
In babies: unusual fussiness, sudden drooling, unusual sleepiness
items.text: If the child has their own prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it straight away, following the device instructions, and then call emergency services at once. If there is no epinephrine, call emergency services at once. Ask for an ambulance, say you think it is anaphylaxis, and say whether epinephrine was given and when. Never use an antihistamine, inhaler or other medicine in place of epinephrine. Keep the child lying down and do not let them stand or walk; if they vomit, turn them onto their side; if they struggle to breathe, tell the call-taker and follow their instructions on position. If symptoms get worse or do not improve within 5 minutes and the child has a second device, a second dose is used, following the child's own plan. Everyone goes to the ER, even if they look better. Dose and device instructions are on the child's own device or plan and are not given here.

signs: Any seizure: call emergency services
Extra warning signs: first ever seizure; lasts longer than 5 minutes; seizures one after another without recovery between them
Child does not wake up afterwards or has trouble breathing
Child was injured, or the seizure happened in water
Child has diabetes or another serious medical condition
items.text: Call emergency services (any seizure). Stay with the child and note the time. Do not hold them down and do not put anything in their mouth. Move hard or sharp things away and cushion the head. Lower them to the ground and, unless a neck or back injury is suspected, onto their side. When the jerking stops, open the airway and check breathing; if they are breathing, use the recovery position, unless a neck or back injury is suspected (then keep holding the head steady and follow step 9).

signs: Large (about the size of the child's palm or bigger) or deep burn
Face, hands, genitals or bottom
Electrical or chemical burn; skin that looks charred, leathery, white, brown or black, or has no feeling
Breathing trouble, smoke or fume exposure, confusion or difficulty waking; or you are not sure how serious it is
Blistering burn bigger than the child's hand, or a burn on a foot or over a joint: seen immediately by a paediatrician or in an emergency room
items.text: If the burn has any of the call-now signs: call emergency services first (put the phone on speaker, or ask someone else to call), then cool the burn while you wait and while on the call. For every burn, cool at once under cool (not icy) running water for 20 minutes. For a burn on the face, apply a cold wet washcloth right away instead. Do not delay cooling to undress the child; remove clothing or jewellery near the burn only if it is not stuck to the skin. Make sure the child does not get too cold: use a coat or blanket to keep them warm if necessary. No ice, butter, creams or oils. After cooling, cover loosely with cling film laid over the burn (not wrapped; not on the face) or a clean, non-fluffy cloth.

signs: Bleeding that will not stop with firm pressure
Blood spurting or hard to control
Deep or large wound, or an object stuck in the wound
Numbness or inability to move near the wound
items.text: Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing at once and keep pressing. Shout for someone to call emergency services; if you are alone, put the phone on speaker and call while you keep pressing. If blood soaks through, put more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is stuck in the wound, leave it and press firmly on either side of it.

Not legal advice. Rules on who can agree to a child's treatment vary by state and by country, and emergency consent rules are not covered here. If you believe a child is in danger, call emergency services; the operator will guide you.

items.topic: Lone rescuer: call first or do CPR first for a child who is unresponsive and not breathing

positions.claim: With a phone: call on speakerphone, then CPR. Alone with no phone: 5 cycles of 30:2 (about 2 minutes) before leaving to call 911. (AHA Heartsaver summary, 2025; the AHA site itself returned an access error, so this is a copy hosted by Vanderbilt University Medical Center.)
The American Red Cross child and baby CPR page puts 'call 9-1-1 and get equipment, or tell someone to do so' before the CPR steps; its 2-minute-then-call line is worded for a baby.
If alone, do about 2 minutes of CPR first, then call (you may carry the child unless spinal injury is suspected). With a second person, one calls while the other starts CPR.
If alone with no phone, give 5 rescue breaths then 1 minute of CPR before calling; with a phone, call on speaker.
If alone, give about 1 minute of CPR before calling; if anyone is with you they call straight away.
Call the ambulance service immediately using the speaker function; a single rescuer without a mobile phone does CPR for 1 minute before going to seek help.

items.note: With a phone: AHA, St John Ambulance and Resuscitation Council UK say call on speaker first and the American Red Cross lists the call first; British Red Cross and MedlinePlus do not mention a phone. Only the no-phone timing differs: about 1 minute (St John Ambulance, British Red Cross, Resuscitation Council UK) versus about 2 minutes (AHA, MedlinePlus). The guide carries 1 minute. Top question for the clinician.

positions.claim: UK guidance (St John Ambulance, British Red Cross) opens with 5 rescue breaths, then 30:2.
MedlinePlus (US) starts with compressions and gives 2 breaths per 30 compressions, with no initial 5 breaths.

items.note: Regional protocol difference; the app needs a clinician decision per region.

items.topic: Seizure: when to call emergency services

positions.claim: Call 911 or 999 for any seizure (rhythmic jerking and loss of responsiveness / a seizure or fit).

The AAP first-aid page says seizures in children usually are not medical emergencies and lists when to call 911: first seizure, over 5 minutes, back-to-back seizures, not waking, injury, trouble breathing, in water, diabetes or another life-threatening condition.
Call for first seizure, repeats, over 5 minutes, or unresponsive over 10 minutes after.
Febrile seizure handout: call 911 if over 3 minutes or the child is under 6 months.
The AAP 'medical emergency' page puts a seizure lasting more than 2 minutes in a child with no seizure history on its emergency room list (the AAP 911 page lists any seizure).

items.note: Pages differ on whether every seizure is a call. The guide carries the call-now rule for any seizure (the most cautious reading). Thresholds of 2, 3 and 5 minutes also appear. Clinician to choose one safe wording.

positions.claim: About 5 minutes of cool running water, in the section on a MINOR burn.
AAP symptom-checker photo captions: cold water for 10 minutes (first and second degree examples) and 20 minutes (thermal burn, 'do not take time to remove clothing').
20 minutes of cool running water, as soon as possible and within 3 hours; remove clothing near the burn unless stuck.
20 to 30 minutes of running water, then cling film.
Healthdirect Australia: cool running water for at least 20 minutes as soon as possible while waiting for an ambulance. MedlinePlus: for a minor burn, 5 to 30 minutes.

items.note: Internal conflict even within the AAP. The guide carries 20 minutes (the figure on two NHS pages and one AAP caption); 5 minutes is stated only for a minor burn. A clinician should confirm.

items.topic: Anaphylaxis: order of epinephrine and the call

positions.claim: Give epinephrine right away, then call 911; give a second dose if symptoms get worse, continue, or do not get better in 5 minutes.
Use the auto-injector, then call 999; second injector if no better after 5 minutes.
Call 911 first, check airway, breathing and circulation, and use epinephrine immediately if available.

items.note: All three sources want the call and the epinephrine within moments of each other. The guide carries one order: epinephrine first if the child has it, then the call at once; with no epinephrine, call at once (MedlinePlus: call 911 immediately; NHS: call 999 if you think it is anaphylaxis). MedlinePlus lists the call first. Whether a second adult should call while the first injects is a clinician question (not stated by the sources). Second dose: AAP gives the trigger as symptoms that get worse, continue or do not get better in 5 minutes; NHS says not improved after 5 minutes.

positions.claim: Keep the child lying on the back; if they vomit or have trouble breathing, keep them lying on their side.
Lie down, legs can be raised; if struggling to breathe, raise the shoulders or sit up slowly; do not stand or walk.
Lie flat with feet raised and cover with a coat or blanket, but do not use this position if a head, neck, back or leg injury is suspected, if it causes discomfort, or if they are vomiting.

items.note: The pages differ. The guide carries: lying down, no standing or walking, side if vomiting, and follow the call-taker if struggling to breathe; it does not tell the reader to raise the legs. Clinician to decide.

positions.claim: AAP: call Poison Help for any suspected poisoning, even with no symptoms. The same AAP page also lists 'ingests something poisonous' among its call-911-immediately items, and lists batteries and magnets among things to call Poison Control about.
Poison.org: call 911 for collapse, seizure, trouble breathing or cannot be woken; otherwise use its online tool or a poison centre.

UK NHS: call 999 or go to A&E if you think a child has swallowed, touched or breathed in something harmful, and 111 only if you are unsure it is harmful. The NHS accident page also lists a swallowed poison or too much medicine under 999, and a swallowed button battery or magnet as 999 or A&E straight away.
Canada (SickKids): do not wait for symptoms; get care from a poison information centre or call 911 right away.

Australia (healthdirect): call 000 if someone stops breathing, collapses, has a seizure, has a severe allergic reaction or has been exposed to a harmful substance; otherwise call 13 11 26. Another line on the same page words it as exposed to a harmful substance AND stops breathing, collapses, has a seizure or an allergic reaction.

items.note: US (poison line first when the child is well) and UK (emergency number if you think it is harmful) differ, so regions need separate wording. Most cautious reading: if the child is unwell or you believe the child is in danger, call emergency services; in Australia, call 000 for exposure to a harmful substance.

items.topic: Is the US 1-800-222-1222 line still answered? (resolved)

positions.claim: Poison.org: the National Capital Poison Center closed its own call centre on 31 March 2025 and became all-digital. Its press release says the toll-free national number still works and that calls from its former area are re-routed to neighbouring poison centres in Maryland and Virginia.
MedlinePlus and America's Poison Centers: the national number reaches local/regional poison centres, free, 24 hours, every day (53 accredited centres).

items.note: Resolved: the number works and is answered by a regional poison centre. The 'unresolved' flag came from reading one centre's closure as the closure of the line. HRSA's page could not be opened.

positions.claim: 100.5 F or higher in a child under 60 days old needs prompt medical care.
Fever above 100.4 F in a child under 60 days old is listed under emergency medical care (ER or 911).

items.note: Within the AAP; the guide carries the more cautious ER reading (see urgentCareOrER). Belongs to the fever guide.

positions.claim: Lower the child to the ground and turn them on their side during the seizure; do not restrain them.
Do not restrain or move the casualty unless in immediate danger; when the jerking stops, open the airway, check breathing and use the recovery position if breathing.

items.note: The guide carries the AAP wording for the seizure and the St John Ambulance steps for after the jerking stops. Clinician to confirm.

items.topic: Tap or shake to check response

positions.claim: Do not shake the child (MedlinePlus).
Gently shake the shoulders (St John Ambulance).

items.note: The guide carries the more cautious reading: call out and tap the shoulder, do not shake.

items.topic: Severe bleeding: press first or call first, and a soaked cloth

positions.claim: For life-threatening bleeding, apply direct pressure to the wound before managing the airway, and call if you have not already. For severe bleeding, control it with direct pressure and call 999 or 112.
Press firmly on the wound; if the bleeding is severe, call 999. If blood soaks through the pad, replace it with a new one if possible.
If blood comes through the bandage or cloth, apply another bandage or cloth on top.

items.note: No opened source says to call before pressing. The guide carries: press firmly at once and shout for someone to call, or call on speaker while pressing if alone; put more cloth on top if soaked. Clinician to confirm.

items.topic: Burn: call first or cool first, cooling a large burn, and the face

positions.claim: Healthdirect Australia lists cooling under 'what to do while waiting for an ambulance' for a burn that needs 000 (deep, face, hands, genitals, chemical, electrical, airway).
NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a very large or deep burn or one on the face, genitals or bottom, and separately says to cool for 20 minutes; it gives no order.

MedlinePlus says to call 911 for a serious burn or one the size of the person's palm or larger, and not to place a severe burn in cold water (it can cause shock); cooling for 5 to 30 minutes is described for minor burns.

AAP symptom checker: for burns on the face, apply a cold wet washcloth right away. AAP first-aid page: a hand-sized blistering burn, or one on the hand, foot, face, genitals or over a joint, should be seen immediately by a paediatrician or in an emergency room.
Healthdirect: do not use plastic cling film if the burn is to the face. NHS: lay cling film over the burn once cooled.

items.note: The guide carries: call (speaker, or ask someone else), then cool while waiting; cold wet washcloth for the face; no cling film on the face; cooling for any burn. MedlinePlus conflicts on cooling a severe burn. Clinician to decide the order and the cooling rule for a large burn.

items: HRSA poisonhelp.hrsa.gov, the original American Heart Association pages (cpr.heart.org) and the CRTC 911 page (crtc.gc.ca) returned HTTP 403 or a security check and were not opened. AHA content here comes from an AHA summary sheet copied onto a university medical-centre site (source 39); confirm against the AHA original.

Canadian emergency 911 is supported only by SickKids (hospital site). A search-result snippet (not opened) suggests some remote Canadian areas lack 911; this is NOT stated in the guide. Canada poison line hours and the 811 nurse line were not confirmed on an opened official page.
A US nurse advice line number (no single national number was found in opened sources).
What to tell a dispatcher about 'what has already been done': no opened source states this explicitly.
Child's weight, insurance information, and named emergency contacts as items for a sitter or grandparent handover: no opened authoritative source covers it.
What to do if you cannot reach a parent: no opened source covers it beyond the AAP advice to phone the child's own paediatrician, even out of hours.
Emergency medical consent law for non-parent caregivers: not covered by opened sources; varies by place. The 'leave written permission' habit is general practice, not sourced.
What an urgent care clinic can and cannot treat for children (US); only the AAP's pointer to another article.
Whether a second adult should call while another gives epinephrine: not stated by any opened source.

US wording for a swallowed button battery or magnet: AAP lists them under Poison Control, NHS says 999/A&E straight away. A US emergency source was not found; the guide carries the NHS reading for the UK only.
Infant (under 1 year) CPR, choking and compression technique: out of scope, not researched. Choking first aid while waiting is also out of scope here.
Epinephrine nasal spray by weight: AAP source 4 says sprays are approved for children weighing 33 pounds or more; no dose or device guidance is given here.

The NHS 'when to call 999' page does not itself say to stay on the line (it says to follow the call handler); that rule rests on the AAP and healthdirect pages. That NHS page showed a review date of February 2023 with the next review due February 2026, so it was overdue when retrieved; the same location and callback items appear on the AAP and healthdirect pages.

No opened page says what to do when the US poison line does not connect and the child looks well. The 911 line rests on the AAP rule to call 911 when you believe a child is in danger. HRSA's page could not be opened. Clinician question.

The order of calling and cooling for a large burn: only healthdirect's 'while waiting for an ambulance' heading implies call, then cool. MedlinePlus says not to put a severe burn in cold water. No source gives an explicit lone-adult order.

Severe bleeding for a lone adult: St John Ambulance says press first and call if you have not already; NHS says call if the bleeding is severe. 'Shout for someone, or call on speaker while pressing' is built from the St John Ambulance primary survey (shout for a helper, or put the phone on speaker and call yourself) and is not stated for bleeding alone.

Seizure and a suspected neck or back injury: 'unless a neck or back injury is suspected' for turning onto the side and for the recovery position is built from the St John Ambulance spinal injury page (do not move unless in danger) combined with the seizure pages; no seizure page states it.
A lone adult with no phone and a suspected neck or back injury: no opened source covers whether to shout for help, leave, or stay.
Whether a family should leave written permission with a sitter or grandparent is general practice; no opened source states it. Needs clinician and legal review.

Scope question, not a verification gap: the 988 Lifeline home page does not mention children; the AAP page (source 3) says parents and caregivers can use 988 for a child or teen in crisis. Whether it belongs in a guide for ages 1 to puberty is a clinician question.
The AAP anaphylaxis page allows a prescribed inhaler or antihistamine in addition to epinephrine; this guide omits that and says never in place of epinephrine (the more cautious reading).
Consent: the AAP article (source 8) is written for paediatric practices and concerns non-urgent care brought by someone other than a legal guardian; it does not set out emergency consent rules.

TOP QUESTION. Lone sitter, child unresponsive and not breathing, NO phone: about 1 minute (St John Ambulance, British Red Cross, Resuscitation Council UK; carried here) or about 2 minutes (AHA, MedlinePlus) of CPR before going to call? With a phone, AHA, St John Ambulance and Resuscitation Council UK say call on speaker first and the American Red Cross lists the call first; British Red Cross and MedlinePlus do not mention a phone. Should US and UK wording differ, including UK 5 rescue breaths first versus US compressions first?

Anaphylaxis: is 'epinephrine first if available, then call at once; with none, call at once' safe wording for a lay sitter, should a second adult call while the first injects, and how should the app handle weight-based devices and a second dose without giving doses? Body position: AAP side-lying versus NHS sitting up if struggling to breathe versus MedlinePlus feet raised, and what a lone adult should do in the first moments before a call-taker is on the line.

Poison: in the US, when should the app say poison line first versus 911, given the AAP lists poisoning in both places, including button batteries and magnets? What should a caregiver do if the poison line does not connect and the child looks well?

Burn: confirm the carried order for a large burn (call on speaker or ask someone else to call, then cool while waiting), the cooling time (20 minutes carried; sources say 5, 10, 20, 20 to 30 or at least 20), cooling at all for a large or severe burn given MedlinePlus says not to put a severe burn in cold water, the palm-sized threshold for calling, a cold wet washcloth for the face, and no cling film on the face. Seizure: confirm call-for-any-seizure against the AAP wording that most seizures are not emergencies, and the neck and back exception to turning on the side.

Severe bleeding for a lone adult: confirm 'press at once and shout for someone to call, or call on speaker while pressing', and whether a lone adult with no phone and a suspected neck or back injury should shout, stay or go.
Consent and unreachable parents: what safe, non-legal wording should the app use, what should a sitter do first if a parent cannot be reached, and does the app need a legal reviewer per region?
US mental health line 988: should a guide for ages 1 to puberty include it, and with what wording?

items.what: US poison line: replaced the 'unresolved' staffing question with the verified statement (national number still works, free, 24/7, routes to regional poison centres; NCPC closed only its own call room on 31 March 2025). Added the fallback: if the child is unwell or you believe the child is in danger, call 911.

Lone-rescuer CPR: with a phone, call on speaker straight away then start CPR (AHA Heartsaver 2025 summary, St John Ambulance, American Red Cross agree). Without a phone the sources give about 1 or about 2 minutes of CPR before going to call: kept as an explicit disagreement and made the top clinician question.
CPR start by region: US sources start with 30 compressions; UK sources start with 5 rescue breaths. No pulse check for lay people (MedlinePlus).

Burn first step now carries a cooling time: 20 minutes as the most cautious reading (NHS, AAP thermal-burn caption), with the 5 / 10 / 20-30 minute disagreement shown. Do not delay cooling to undress; electrical and chemical burns go to emergency care per NHS.

Anaphylaxis: epinephrine and the call both straight away (AAP and NHS: inject, then call at once; MedlinePlus lists the call first); never use an antihistamine or inhaler instead of epinephrine; say it is anaphylaxis and say epinephrine was given and when; do not stand or walk; no doses.
UK poison row rewritten to match NHS: 999 or A&E if you think a child swallowed, touched or breathed in something harmful; 111 if unsure whether it is harmful. Removed 'odd sounds, colour change'.
Neck or back injury: jaw lift without tilting the head (St John Ambulance, MedlinePlus); head-tilt step made conditional; removed 'you may have to move them'.
Canada: removed the claim that Canadian sources say the same as Australia. SickKids says get advice from a poison information centre or call 911 without waiting for symptoms.
Deleted the unsourced 'extra questions do not delay the ambulance' clause and the unsourced 'do not wait for a parent, doctor or form' line.

Baby fever row moved out of the doctor-or-nurse-line list into the ER list (AAP 'Is it a medical emergency' lists fever above 100.4 F under 60 days as emergency care); disagreement with the 100.5 F prompt-care line kept.
Consent wording: AAP source is written for practices and covers non-urgent visits; 'leave written permission' is now labelled general practice, not from the source.
All 'not verified' items moved out of the advice arrays into 'unverified'.

Citation fixes: 112 in the UK now cites St John Ambulance; 000/112 cites healthdirect pages that say it; Canada 911 cites SickKids (CRTC page blocked, not used); poisoncontrol.org relabelled; HRSA and original AHA pages listed as not opened.
Emergency-now list reworded so it no longer follows the AAP list line by line; added NHS and AAP items (altered alertness, severe pain, heat or cold injury, swallowed poison per NHS).
Added: tap the shoulders, do not shake; turn on inside and outside lights and unlock the front door; Australia cannot text 000.
Recovery position: step 5 now applies only when no neck or back injury is suspected; step 9 says to keep supporting the head and monitor if unresponsive but breathing (St John Ambulance spinal page).

Seizure: one rule, call emergency services for any seizure (AAP and NHS call-now lists); extra features kept as warning signs; AAP 'usually not emergencies' position and the moving-the-child difference added to disagreements; ER list no longer carries a 2-minute exception.
Burn: added keep the child warm (NHS accident page, burns paragraph; earlier decline reversed after reading the raw page).

Anaphylaxis: one lying-down rule (side if vomiting, follow the call-taker if struggling to breathe), position differences moved to a new disagreement row; removed the 'other prescribed medicine' parenthesis and the 'no delay' gloss.
JSON and Markdown made identical in substance (Australia 112 fallback, ER wording, parenthesis).
Poison: added Australia 000 for exposure to a harmful substance, SickKids altered-awareness line, US 988 line (AAP page and 988lifeline.org), and a poison disagreement position.
Removed source caveats from advice strings (moved to unverified); reworded poison-line status to what the retrieved pages say; stay-on-the-line wording now follows the AAP with the operator release.
Added Resuscitation Council UK 2025 paediatric BLS (speaker call; 1 minute with no phone) as source 42; no-phone step now carries 1 minute with the 2-minute position in disagreements.

Round 3 corrections. Severe bleeding: removed the unsupported 'call, then press' order; now press firmly at once and shout for someone to call, or call on speaker while pressing; source difference moved to a new disagreement row. Burns: one call list used in sections 1, 4 and 7 (added hands, bottom, palm-sized, charred or colour change, unsure); order for a large burn (call on speaker or ask someone, then cool while waiting); cold wet washcloth for the face; no cling film on the face; new sources 43 (healthdirect burns) and 44 (MedlinePlus burns); MedlinePlus 'no cold water on a severe burn' shown as a disagreement and clinician question. Anaphylaxis: one order (epinephrine then call; with none, call at once); second-dose trigger is symptoms that get worse or do not improve within 5 minutes. 'Cannot speak' changed to 'trouble speaking'. Top clinician question no longer claims every authority says call first. Seizure: AAP emergency-room-list qualifier restored; neck or back exception added to the side-lying and recovery steps. Failed poison-line connection with a well child flagged, not invented. Source commentary, 'see disagreements', 'see section' and 'AAP says' removed from advice strings; the unsourced 'leave written permission' sentence moved to unverified; Markdown regenerated from the JSON so both are identical in substance.
